lifeplan / every combination of five conditions / example

1,176 scenarios you might (or might not) follow

For an average, invented household, every combination of three conditions you decide and two you cannot was turned into a scenario, 1,176 in all. Under some conditions the household goes bankrupt. The point of computing every combination is to see which conditions shape the path of the assets, and by how much.

How this simulator computes

Pick one option from each of several conditions, and the simulator computes the path of the assets year by year, adding up the pay, the pension, tax, social insurance, the living cost, the rent or the mortgage, and the return on what is held. That shows the future those choices lead to. Running it for every combination of every option of every condition shows how much each condition matters. The lines in the next figure are the balance of the assets deflated to 2022 prices. The year a line drops below zero is the year the assets run out; we call it the ruin year.

What conditions were assumed

Computing every combination of the conditions shows which option to take.

There are two kinds: conditions nobody controls (prices, wage growth, investment returns, the timing of a crash) and decisions (housing, work, spending, children's schooling, when to draw the pension). Computing a scenario for each combination shows which decisions matter.

Which condition moves the result

Effect size of each condition (η², share of variance explained)

Roughly, the effect size is how much a condition matters. Precisely, it is the share of the variance of the final assets that the differences between the means of that condition's options account for. A condition whose options barely move the mean has a small effect size.

The economy is not a choice

For each economy, every combination of the other four conditions

In the harshest economy (ゼロ成長枯渇), 96.4% of combinations fail. Only the most favourable settings of the household's decisions survive there. This is the sweep's most useful output: it shows how much of the problem is outside what the household can choose.

Each decision on its own

Median net worth and ruin rate for each option, across every combination of the other conditions

Where the rows of a table barely differ, that decision barely matters for this household: 年金受給開始 accounts for under 1% of the variance. That is a result too. It says which questions the household can stop deliberating over, and which one (住まい) deserves the time.

Housing and living cost together

Each row covers every combination of the other three conditions

What happens after the money runs out

When the assets run out, the household either sells the home and rents, or borrows against it

Both require the mortgage to be repaid first. A home already pledged cannot be pledged again, so selling means clearing the loan out of the proceeds. Both are evaluated and the better one is taken.

Running it on your own conditions

The simulator and the full-combination run are in the repository, and nothing in them is specific to this household. Three things change:

  1. Describe the household. Income, spending, housing, loans, pension and so on are one TSV file each under data/controllable/; the manifest projects/base.tsv lists which file fills which slot. Replace the figures with your own. The README in that directory says where each of the example figures came from.
  2. Write the options. Each option is another TSV file for the same slot; the ones used here are under data/controllable/scenario/ (decisions) and data/environment/scenario/ (economies, crashes).
  3. List the conditions. Axes() in tools/sweep/main.go names each condition, its options, and which file each option swaps in. Add, remove or rename conditions there. The number of plans to run is the product of the option counts.

Then run the three commands in the footer. The sweep runs one plan per combination on every core; the two scripts produce this page from the results.

Generated by tools/sweep, which passes overrides to plan.Build instead of writing 1,176 manifests. Results are in out/sweep/cells.tsv. Reproduce with go run ./tools/sweep && python3 docs/analyse.py && python3 docs/build.py.

The household in this report does not exist. Nobody lives on exactly these figures, but each figure comes from a published statistic. The salary comes from the 民間給与実態統計調査 by age band, the spouse's pay from the 賃金構造基本統計調査 hourly rate for part-time women, the spending from the 家計調査 for the head's age band, and the rent and purchase price from the going rate for a 70㎡ flat in 八王子市. Each source is cited in data/controllable/README.md. Only the household's makeup is invented; the decisions, the statutory rules and the economic projections are real. All amounts are in real terms, discounted to the plan's first year. Pension levels follow the 2024 財政検証. The crash size is a round figure chosen by hand rather than derived from any particular portfolio.
